newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac seeks to calm self-made EMU row with Italy.
newsitem.headline: Chirac seeks to calm self-made EMU row with Italy.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac sparked a diplomatic storm with Rome on Tuesday by casting doubt on Italy's fitness to be a founder member of a single European currency in 1999, and was forced to back down.

Chirac triggered the row in talking to businessmen in the depressed textile town of Arras when, blaming a devalued lira for some of the French textile sector's woes, he suggested Rome might not qualify for the first wave of European monetary union.

"Things are going to go pretty quickly now, on January 1, 1999, for some countries which will have made the effort to clean up their economic and financial situation...It may take a little bit longer for those who are further behind, like Italy," he said.

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi summoned the French ambassador and, according to sources in both Rome and Paris, threatened to call off a Franco-Italian summit set for Thursday and Friday in Naples unless Chirac retracted.
The French leader swiftly rowed back, telling a news conference: "Italy...is conducting a courageous policy which is bearing fruit.

"I believe the Italian government is fully determined to do everything, as it has shown in its budget, to be in the first wave of countries to join the euro. Of course, I ardently hope it will succeed."
French officials acknowledged that Chirac's earlier comments had been a "gaffe" and sought to minimise their impact.
Ironically, it was Chirac who cancelled last year's Franco-Italian summit in anger at Rome's criticism of French nuclear weapons testing in the South Pacific.
The atmosphere at this week's meeting could be electric.

The president tread on more thin ice by saying he had been among the first "to rejoice at the change of Italian government on seeing the arrival of a team which seemed determined to fight against these lax tendencies".
Previous prime minister Lamberto Dini, whose relations with the French leader were frosty, is still foreign minister.
The row came at the worst time for Italy after the government announced a tougher-than-expected austerity budget to try to meet the Maastricht treaty criteria for joining the euro.

Italian deputy prime minister Walter Veltroni accused Chirac of grave interference in Italy's affairs and Treasury and Budget Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, speaking in Washington, said no country had the right to pass judgement on others.
Chirac's initial comments briefly caused the lira to fall against the deutschmark, although it recovered as analysts reckoned he had done little more than state the obvious.
He said it was "quite obvious that the lira's movement is completely incompatible with a single European market, even if it has rebounded slightly recently".
A fixed link between the euro and the currencies of non-founder members of the European unit was an "unavoidable" necessity, he added.
Chirac's comments could fuel fears in Italy and Spain that some European states, notably economic powerhouse Germany, are actively trying to bar them from being a founder of the euro.
A defiant Prodi told reporters in Rome that some partners, including France and Germany, were motivated by fear of competition from dynamic Italian industry.
